# New Paradigm of Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education and Teaching: An Evidence-Based, Practice-Oriented Research Paper

The strongest conclusion is that holistic empowerment should be presented as a carefully bounded synthesis rather than as an already validated educational model. It brings together language proficiency, learner agency, social-emotional development, inclusion, creativity, cultural identity, authentic communication, and teacher reflection. Evidence from elementary English classrooms, curriculum documents, case studies, reviews, and quasi-experimental studies supports many of these components, but no retrieved study validates one integrated construct named exactly “New Paradigm of Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education and Teaching.” The practical implication is clear: teachers should retain explicit language teaching while creating structured opportunities for children to choose, collaborate, communicate, create, reflect, and use English meaningfully.

This paper first defines the proposed paradigm and distinguishes it from drill-centred or narrowly language-only teaching. It then explains its theoretical foundations, organizes its principal dimensions, examines documented classroom examples, offers an evidence-informed progression for novice teachers, and discusses assessment, feasibility, limitations, and professional learning.

## Abstract

Elementary English education is increasingly expected to develop more than vocabulary, grammar, and the four language skills. It is also expected to support communication, confidence, self-directed learning, collaboration, creativity, cultural understanding, social-emotional growth, and equitable participation. This paper proposes “holistic empowerment” as an author-synthesized framework for connecting these aims in elementary English education and teaching.

Holistic empowerment is defined here as the sustained expansion of children’s capacity and opportunity to use English to understand, communicate, choose, collaborate, create, reflect, and act, supported by explicit language instruction, appropriate scaffolding, inclusive design, and responsive assessment. The framework draws on whole-child education, learner agency, communicative and task-based language teaching, content and language integrated learning, concept-based instruction, project-based learning, culturally responsive pedagogy, social-emotional learning, universal design for learning, formative assessment, and teacher reflective practice.

The evidence base is diverse. Official curriculum guidance emphasizes whole-person development, student-centred learning, learner diversity, multimodal literacy, task-based learning, self-directed learning, and assessment for and as learning. Elementary studies report promising findings for integrated instruction, social-emotional learning, action-based learning, project work, digital storytelling, differentiated instruction, and portfolio assessment. However, much of the evidence is based on small samples, single schools, qualitative perceptions, conceptual frameworks, or short interventions. Digital storytelling, project-based learning, inclusive assessment, and mentoring all show practical benefits alongside important constraints.

The paper argues that empowerment does not mean removing teacher direction. The teacher remains responsible for designing access, modelling language, establishing routines, organizing interaction, monitoring participation, and providing feedback. For novice teachers, the paradigm is most feasible when introduced gradually: establish a safe language-rich routine, select one language objective and one empowerment goal, scaffold participation, offer limited choices, create an authentic product, collect formative evidence, and reflect before expanding to a short project. The central recommendation is therefore not to abandon systematic language teaching, but to make language learning more purposeful, participatory, inclusive, reflective, and connected to children’s lives.

## Keywords

Holistic empowerment; elementary English education; elementary English teaching; whole-child development; whole-person development; learner agency; learner autonomy; communicative competence; task-based language teaching; project-based learning; content and language integrated learning; concept-based instruction; social-emotional learning; inclusive pedagogy; differentiated instruction; Universal Design for Learning; translanguaging; multiliteracies; multimodal literacy; culturally responsive pedagogy; funds of knowledge; formative assessment; assessment as learning; portfolio assessment; teacher reflection; action research; novice teacher development; mentoring; professional learning communities.

## 1. Introduction: Why Elementary English Education Needs Holistic Empowerment

### 1.1 The problem behind the new paradigm

Elementary English classrooms are often asked to achieve several goals at once. Children need to develop listening, speaking, reading, writing, pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, and literacy strategies. At the same time, they are expected to become confident communicators, cooperative classmates, independent learners, thoughtful users of information, and respectful participants in diverse communities.

A narrow language model treats these aims as separate or places language form at the centre of nearly every decision. Lessons may move from explanation to repetition, from individual completion to marking, with communication reduced to the production of predetermined sentences. Such lessons can be efficient for introducing a language pattern, and explicit practice remains necessary for young learners. The problem arises when controlled practice becomes the dominant experience and children have few opportunities to use English for purposes that matter to them.

A broader educational view recognizes that language learning is social, emotional, cognitive, and cultural. The Learning Policy Institute defines whole-child education as an approach that attends to children’s social, emotional, cognitive, academic, physical, and mental-health development, supported by safe environments and rich learning experiences inside and outside school [Learning Policy Institute’s whole-child education framework](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/topic/whole-child-education). The 2025 Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide similarly positions primary English as a context for language proficiency, personal and intellectual development, cultural understanding, generic skills, values, attitudes, self-directed learning, and lifelong learning [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, Primary 1–6 (2025)](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

These directions do not mean that every English lesson must become a large project or a counselling session. They mean that language development should be designed in ways that respect the whole learner.

### 1.2 Working definition

The exact phrase “New Paradigm of Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education and Teaching” is not established in the supplied literature as a source-defined and empirically validated model. The term is therefore used in this paper as a transparent working construct.

Holistic empowerment in elementary English education means:

> the sustained expansion of children’s capacity and opportunity to use English to understand, communicate, choose, collaborate, create, reflect, and act, while developing language knowledge and skills through explicit teaching, meaningful contexts, inclusive participation, and responsive feedback.

This definition contains five important qualifications.

First, empowerment includes language development. A child cannot be empowered by being invited to speak without receiving the vocabulary, sentence frames, pronunciation support, reading strategies, and rehearsal time needed to participate.

Second, empowerment is relational. It depends not only on the child’s motivation but also on teacher expectations, classroom relationships, peer norms, materials, assessment, and school conditions.

Third, empowerment is structured. Children receive meaningful choices within clear boundaries. They may choose a topic, example, role, product, or presentation mode, but they still work toward shared learning goals.

Fourth, empowerment is inclusive. It asks whether all children can enter the task, understand the instructions, contribute to the group, and demonstrate learning in more than one form.

Fifth, empowerment is developmental. An eight-year-old and an eleven-year-old should not be expected to exercise agency in identical ways. Young learners require more modelling, physical support, visual cues, predictable routines, and teacher guidance before they can manage more independent choices.

### 1.3 Central thesis

The central thesis of this paper is:

> Elementary English education becomes more educationally powerful when language learning is organized as a language-rich, inclusive, and scaffolded process through which children develop communicative competence together with agency, social-emotional capacity, creativity, cultural connection, and responsibility for learning.

This is not a claim that holistic empowerment has already been proven as one unified intervention. It is a synthesis of established and emerging practices whose individual elements have different levels of evidence.

### 1.4 How the paradigm differs from narrower approaches

The difference is best understood as a change in the relationship among language, learner, teacher, and evidence.

A narrow language-only model may ask: “Did the child remember the target words and produce the correct sentence?” A holistic empowerment model also asks: “Can the child use those words for a meaningful purpose, listen to another person, make a contribution, revise an idea, and recognize what helped the learning?”

A drill-centred model may treat mistakes primarily as failures of accuracy. A holistic model treats errors as information: they may indicate missing vocabulary, insufficient processing time, weak confidence, unclear task design, or a need for additional visual or peer support.

A teacher-controlled model may define participation as compliance. A holistic model defines participation as purposeful involvement, while retaining the teacher’s responsibility for safety, access, pacing, and instructional clarity.

A product-focused model may assess the final poster, paragraph, or speech. A holistic model also examines planning, rehearsal, collaboration, revision, reflection, and individual progress.

The distinction should not be exaggerated. Traditional instruction contains valuable practices, including explicit explanation, repetition, phonics, vocabulary review, and carefully sequenced grammar teaching. Holistic empowerment is not a replacement for these practices. It is a different way of deciding when and why to use them.

## 2. Conceptual and Research Foundations

### 2.1 Whole-child and whole-person education

Whole-child education provides the broadest foundation. Its central insight is that academic learning is connected to relationships, emotional security, identity, health, and meaningful experience. Safe and welcoming environments are not decorative additions to instruction; they affect whether children are willing to take linguistic risks, ask for help, persist through difficulty, and listen to others.

The Whole Child Policy Toolkit describes trust, strong relationships, and a sense of being valued as conditions that support healthy learning and development [Whole Child Policy Toolkit](https://www.wholechildpolicy.org/). In an English classroom, these conditions have a direct linguistic function. A child who fears public correction may avoid speaking. A child who does not understand classroom routines may spend cognitive energy interpreting the situation rather than processing English. A child who sees the language classroom as a place where home language, accent, or cultural knowledge is treated as a deficit may participate only minimally.

The whole-child perspective therefore changes the teacher’s first question. Instead of asking only whether a lesson contains enough language input, the teacher asks whether the environment enables children to use that input.

The Learning Policy Institute also emphasizes that whole-child education requires relationship-centred environments, deeper-learning curriculum and assessment, integrated supports, educator preparation, and systemic policymaking. This is important because a classroom teacher cannot solve every barrier alone. A holistic paradigm must recognize the influence of timetable, class size, curriculum demands, special educational needs provision, family communication, school leadership, and assessment policy.

### 2.2 Elementary English as a multidimensional curriculum

The 2025 Hong Kong guide provides a particularly clear official example of multidimensional English education. It organizes the subject around three interrelated strands:

- the Interpersonal Strand, using English to establish relationships, exchange ideas, and get things done;
- the Knowledge Strand, using English to find, interpret, organize, and apply information and solve problems; and
- the Experience Strand, using English to respond to and express real and imaginative experiences.

The guide also identifies communication, critical thinking, creativity, problem solving, self-management, self-learning, information technology, mathematical, and collaboration skills as generic skills developed through English learning. Its curriculum framework connects knowledge and skills with values and attitudes rather than treating them as unrelated additions [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, Primary 1–6 (2025)](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

This model is useful for the present paper because it gives a practical answer to a common concern: how can a teacher attend to whole-child development without losing the subject? The answer is to design English tasks in which language is the means through which children communicate, investigate, interpret, imagine, and act.

### 2.3 Learner agency, autonomy, and teacher power

Learner agency refers to a learner’s capacity to participate intentionally, make choices, use strategies, influence activity, and reflect on consequences. Learner autonomy refers more specifically to taking responsibility for aspects of one’s learning, such as setting goals, selecting resources, monitoring progress, and evaluating performance.

Agency is not the same as unrestricted choice. Young learners need teachers to model choices, narrow alternatives, make expectations visible, and provide language for participation.

Tsai’s 2025 conceptual framework for elementary EFL combines Learner-Generated Contexts and generative AI within a collaborative, scaffolded environment. It identifies four components: learner autonomy and agency; teacher-guided scaffolded learning; a collaborative learning environment; and assessment and evaluation [Tsai’s conceptual framework for learner-generated contexts in elementary EFL](https://journal.uii.ac.id/JEE/article/view/40446). The structure is valuable because it rejects a false opposition between teacher authority and learner agency. Agency grows through guidance that eventually becomes less necessary, not through the sudden removal of guidance.

The limitation is equally important: Tsai’s article proposes a framework but does not report empirical outcome evaluation. It should therefore be used as a conceptual foundation and planning lens, not as proof that one particular model improves elementary outcomes.

Research on teacher power also provides a useful caution. Diaz, Cochran, and Karlin studied English language learners’ perceptions of teacher power and learner empowerment using quantitative measures and twenty in-depth interviews. Their interview themes concerned what good teachers do, what bad teachers do, what teachers should know, and the importance of understanding ELL students [Diaz, Cochran, and Karlin on teacher power and learner empowerment](https://doi.org/10.1080/87567555.2015.1126801). Although the study was not an elementary intervention, it shows why empowerment cannot be reduced to a set of activities. Students interpret how teachers use authority. Clear expectations can communicate care and competence; coercion, humiliation, or inflexible control can communicate that students have little legitimate voice.

### 2.4 From skills and facts to concepts, transfer, and action

Concept-based instruction offers one way to move beyond isolated topic coverage. A 2026 collective case study examined ten Taiwanese elementary English teachers implementing concept-based instruction in natural classrooms. The study contrasts a traditional topic- or skill-based model organized around skills and facts with a three-dimensional model in which learners should know factually, understand conceptually, and be able to act skillfully [Curriculum Perspectives study of concept-based instruction in Taiwanese elementary English classrooms](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41297-026-00343-z).

The distinction is practical. Knowing the words “mix,” “red,” “yellow,” and “orange” is factual knowledge. Understanding that combining elements can produce a new result is conceptual understanding. Explaining or demonstrating the process in a new context is skillful action and transfer.

The Taiwanese teachers used vocabulary review, storytelling, videos, listening clips, hands-on activities, group work, and individual tasks. Across the ten observed lessons, six teachers designed group work, four used hands-on tasks, and four included individual tasks. Examples included colour mixing, paper constructions, magnetic-force experiments, and repairing a broken toy. The study also reports three recurrent challenges: limited English, the need for more scaffolding, and uncertainty about whether students understood the concept. Teachers responded by simplifying classroom language and worksheets, teaching digital tools before requiring students to use them, and guiding learners through concrete demonstrations.

The evidence remains bounded. Each teacher implemented one concept-based lesson and was observed once during the semester. The study illustrates how teachers reasoned about concept-based teaching; it does not establish long-term superiority over other approaches.

### 2.5 Communicative, task-based, and integrated language teaching

Communicative competence involves more than producing grammatically correct sentences. It includes understanding purpose, audience, interaction, meaning, appropriateness, repair, and the social consequences of language use.

McMurray’s account of Korean elementary English reform describes a historical movement from grammar-translation to audio-lingual approaches and then toward communicative teaching. The reform responded to concern that students could demonstrate structural knowledge but struggled to sustain conversation. The 1995 curriculum ranked speaking as the most important of the four skills, promoted learning by doing, and encouraged small-group activity. However, the account also cautioned that Korean elementary English had been implemented for only three years at the time, so its effects were too early to judge [McMurray, “Elementary Education Reforms in Korea”](https://jalt-publications.org/tlt/articles/2382-elementary-education-reforms-korea).

This historical example demonstrates two points. First, educational reform often develops in response to a genuine limitation of the previous model. Second, a change in official language or classroom technique does not itself prove success.

The 2025 Hong Kong guide recommends task-based learning because tasks give students a purpose, context, mode of thinking and doing, process, and product. It also emphasizes that tasks should be purposeful, authentic or close to real life, adaptable to different abilities, and connected with communicative use of English [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, Chapter 4](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

Fortuna and Ching report a significant effect of an integrative approach on elementary learners’ English proficiency in reading, speaking, and writing. Their recommendations include thematic teaching, learning by design, content-based instruction, and scaffolded knowledge integration through planning episodes such as priming, motivation, analysis, abstraction, and application [Fortuna and Ching, “Praxis of Integrative Approach”](https://www.ejournals.ph/article.php?id=27157). The abstract supplied for this study does not provide enough methodological detail to determine the exact sample, effect size, or comparison condition. Its contribution is therefore best treated as supportive evidence for integrative design rather than a complete causal test of holistic empowerment.

### 2.6 Content and language integrated learning

Content and Language Integrated Learning, or CLIL, teaches content and language simultaneously through another language. Kim and Huh explain CLIL through Coyle and colleagues’ 4Cs framework: content, communication, cognition, and culture [Kim and Huh on character-integrated CLIL](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1466862.pdf).

This framework is relevant to holistic empowerment because children use English to learn about something, not merely to practise English forms. Content provides a reason to communicate; communication gives language a social purpose; cognition asks children to notice, compare, predict, or solve; and culture connects learning to perspectives and identity.

In Kim and Huh’s 2025 mixed-method study, eight eight-year-old EFL children—five girls and three boys—participated in sixteen sessions of character-integrated CLIL. The programme focused on sharing and respect, with two eighty-minute classes per week. Each class included circle time, two small-group periods, story time, and a closing phase. Observations, interviews, portfolios, self-assessments, peer assessments, questionnaires, and English tests were used. The authors reported improvements in oral language, confidence, engagement, language proficiency, subject knowledge, and positive character traits.

The study has serious limits: the children were conveniently selected, taught in one class, and not compared with a separate control group. It demonstrates a feasible design and a set of reported outcomes, not general proof. For novice teachers, the practical lesson is to begin with a small content connection—such as food, animals, local places, or classroom science—rather than attempting to turn every English lesson into a full CLIL programme.

### 2.7 Social-emotional learning

Social-emotional learning, or SEL, involves abilities such as recognizing emotions, managing attention and behaviour, showing empathy, building relationships, making responsible decisions, and working with others.

In a quasi-experimental study, 110 Grade 5 students in rural Dong Thap Province, Vietnam, participated in a twelve-week intervention integrating SEL into English lessons using the Grade 5 Global Success textbook. Pre- and post-tests addressed listening, speaking, reading, and writing, and interviews involved eight randomly selected students from four classes. The report found statistically significant academic improvements and described gains in active listening, empathy, helping and cooperating in group work, motivation, and self-discipline [Dong Thap University Journal of Science study of SEL-integrated English teaching](https://dthujs.vn/index.php/dthujs/article/view/2880).

The study is promising but its supplied summary does not provide the exact effect sizes or enough detail about the comparison condition. Its findings support integration, not the claim that every SEL activity automatically improves English.

Zhang and Meng’s Chinese primary-school case study, based on interviews with three English teachers and classroom observations, identified student disengagement, proficiency differences, and outdated instructional approaches as key challenges. After implementing an SEL-English curriculum based on the five CASEL competencies, observations indicated improved engagement, peer collaboration, and language participation. The authors connect self-awareness and self-management activities with attention difficulties and structured peer support with proficiency differences [Zhang and Meng on integrated SEL-English teaching](https://ie.cscholar.com/article/view/1000100). Because the study reports teacher and observational evidence without numerical effect sizes or a stated student sample, its claims should be interpreted as case-based rather than broadly causal.

## 3. Core Dimensions and Principles of Holistic Empowerment

Holistic empowerment can be organized into seven connected dimensions. The dimensions are not separate programmes. In a well-designed task, one activity may develop several at once.

| Dimension | What students experience | Teacher practices | Evidence boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Language and cognitive empowerment | English helps them understand, explain, compare, solve, and transfer ideas | Explicit modelling, contextualized grammar and vocabulary, concept-based tasks | Strong curriculum and case support; integrated construct not validated |
| Agency and self-efficacy | They make bounded choices, set goals, take risks, and see progress | Choice boards, rehearsal, self-assessment, gradual release | Promising quasi-experimental and conceptual evidence |
| Social-emotional and relational growth | They feel safe, listen, cooperate, empathize, and persist | Predictable routines, emotional check-ins, structured collaboration | Elementary studies are promising but heterogeneous |
| Inclusion and access | Different learners can enter, participate, and demonstrate learning | UDL, differentiation, MTSS, multimodal input and output | Implementation often remains uneven |
| Cultural and community connection | Home languages, local knowledge, family experience, and community issues count as resources | Funds-of-knowledge tasks, local texts, family participation | Strong illustrative cases; context-sensitive and time-intensive |
| Creativity and multimodal expression | Students imagine, design, perform, record, draw, and revise | Storytelling, drama, digital or low-tech composition, open-ended products | Engagement evidence exceeds achievement evidence |
| Teacher professional empowerment | Teachers exercise informed judgment and improve practice collaboratively | Reflection, action research, mentoring, PLCs, collaborative planning | Professional-learning evidence is stronger than direct student-outcome evidence |

### 3.1 Language and cognitive empowerment

The first responsibility of holistic English education is still language. Children need repeated encounters with comprehensible input, opportunities to notice patterns, meaningful practice, and feedback that helps them become more accurate and fluent.

The difference lies in how language is selected and used. A vocabulary list becomes more powerful when words are needed to complete a task. Grammar becomes more memorable when it helps children express a real preference, describe an observed process, invite someone, or explain a choice. Reading becomes more purposeful when the information is used to design a poster, solve a problem, or prepare a presentation.

The 2025 Hong Kong guide advises teachers to introduce vocabulary in context through reading, listening, multimodal texts, tasks, and language games rather than relying on decontextualized lists. It also treats grammar as a means to an end, best learned in meaningful contexts where learners can connect form and function [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

A senior teacher’s practical rule is therefore: teach the language children need before and during the task, but do not allow the language lesson to end when the worksheet is complete. The important question is whether learners can carry the language into a new context.

### 3.2 Agency and self-efficacy

Agency becomes visible when children make decisions, initiate communication, use strategies, ask for help, revise work, or take responsibility for a group role. Self-efficacy is the learner’s belief that effort and strategy can lead to improvement.

A useful progression is:

1. The teacher offers one clear model.
2. Students practise with a partner.
3. Students choose among a small number of supported options.
4. Students create or adapt a response.
5. Students explain what they chose and why.
6. Students identify a next step.

This progression is more realistic than asking young children to “take ownership” without teaching them how.

A 2026 quasi-experimental study evaluated Action-Based Learning with gamified digital tools among fifty Grade 5 students, twenty-five in each group. The experimental group showed reported gains of 1.30 on a self-confidence measure and 1.25 on an English-speaking-skills measure, both with reported p-values below .001. Post-test comparisons also favoured the experimental group for confidence, $`t = 4.51, p \lt  .001`$, and oral performance, $`t = 3.35, p = .0012`$ [Zahroni, Syaifuddin, and Khozin on Action-Based Learning](https://doi.org/10.33578/jpfkip.v15i1.94-105).

The authors describe iterative act-and-reflect cycles and Wordwall-supported participation as mechanisms that may reduce foreign-language speaking anxiety and strengthen communicative competence and self-efficacy. The study is quasi-experimental and uses a small sample, so it supports a promising relationship rather than a universal effect.

### 3.3 Social-emotional and relational empowerment

Children speak more when they believe that their contributions will be heard and that mistakes will not produce humiliation. Social-emotional empowerment therefore begins with classroom trust.

The teacher can create this environment through routines that reduce uncertainty, partner rehearsal before public speaking, sentence stems for disagreement, explicit teaching of turn-taking, and feedback that separates the child from the error. “That sentence needs another verb” communicates something very different from “You are careless.”

The classroom should also teach emotional and relational language directly:

- “I feel nervous.”
- “Can you say it again?”
- “I agree because…”
- “I have another idea.”
- “Can you help me?”
- “Let’s give everyone a turn.”
- “I understand your point, but…”

These expressions simultaneously develop English and social participation.

The Dong Thap study provides elementary evidence that SEL can be integrated into English lessons. The broader literature is less direct. A systematic review of twenty-eight articles on social-emotional competence in elementary science education reported pathways through motivation, emotional regulation, perseverance, social interaction, classroom climate, and inquiry engagement. The review is relevant as an adjacent whole-child foundation, but it concerns science rather than elementary English and does not establish an English-specific effect [Systematic review of social-emotional competence in elementary science education](https://doi.org/10.20961/shes.v9i1.117890).

### 3.4 Inclusion and access

Inclusion means more than placing diverse children in the same room. It requires the design of tasks, materials, grouping, assessment, and classroom communication so that diverse learners can participate meaningfully.

Universal Design for Learning, or UDL, commonly emphasizes multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. A 2026 qualitative case study in an inclusive elementary school in Yogyakarta found contextual use of UDL through games, participatory activities, and multimodal resources. However, the action-and-expression component remained limited because assessment was still dominated by standardized written tests [Khasanah and colleagues on UDL in elementary English instruction](http://journal.iistr.org/index.php/IJLREE/article/view/2251).

This finding exposes a common contradiction: teachers may diversify instruction but return to a narrow assessment at the end. If children can learn through images, movement, discussion, and demonstration but can show success only through a written test, the curriculum remains only partially inclusive.

A broader umbrella review of differentiated instruction in inclusive English classrooms reported positive effects across grammar, reading, speaking, writing, motivation, engagement, and social integration. It identified content and process differentiation as particularly consistent across the synthesized studies [Umbrella review of differentiated instruction in inclusive English classrooms](https://bulletin-pedagogic-sc.kaznu.kz/index.php/1-ped/en/article/view/2914). Because this is a synthesis of reviews and meta-analyses rather than one elementary intervention, it supports a general direction but does not provide a single classroom prescription.

The Multi-Tiered System of Support, or MTSS, provides another practical structure. It includes universal Tier 1 support for all learners, targeted Tier 2 support for some learners, and intensive Tier 3 support for learners requiring sustained individualized assistance [Instructional Science study of MTSS and TPRS in elementary EFL](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3).

The same study describes Teaching Proficiency through Reading and Storytelling, or TPRS, as a three-step routine:

1. introduce vocabulary through movement;
2. create a story collaboratively through questioning and student engagement; and
3. read and retell the story.

A three-year design-based study followed a cohort of twenty students in a rural boarding elementary school in southeast China. The teacher used MTSS and TPRS-informed inclusive pedagogy, teaching 35-minute lessons three times per week in Grade 1, four times per week in Grade 2, and daily in Grade 3. The report describes benefits for high-, mid-, and low-performing learners, as well as the importance of teacher collaboration and parental involvement. Its limitations include changing cohort membership and the first author’s simultaneous role as teacher and researcher.

The practical principle is simple: access should be planned before difficulty becomes failure.

### 3.5 Cultural and community empowerment

Children’s lives outside school are not distractions from learning. They are sources of language, knowledge, identity, examples, questions, and motivation.

A 2024 Indonesian research-and-development study designed a local-culture English syllabus for Grade 4 learners in Malang Municipality. Needs assessment involved six English teachers and six school stakeholders. The study reports that local-culture content created familiar contexts associated with improved comprehension, but it also notes that local materials were limited and difficult for teachers to disseminate [Cogent Education study of a local-culture English syllabus](https://doi.org/10.1080/2331186x.2024.2440177).

The study recommends cultural storytelling, community interviews, documentation of local events, and project-based learning connected with students’ heritage. It also reports that performance-based tasks such as cultural presentations and community-event reports were effective for demonstrating language skills. These are valuable examples, but local culture should not be reduced to decorative festivals. The task should allow children to investigate, explain, compare, interpret, or create.

A related Sumbawa module-development study embedded traditional crafts, community activities, and local narratives in Grade 4 English under Indonesia’s Merdeka Curriculum. Expert and practitioner validation produced an average score of 85.7%. That figure is evidence that the module was judged appropriate after revision; it is not evidence of student learning gains, because the authors explicitly call for further field-testing [Sumbawa culturally responsive English module study](https://journal.pcn.ac.id/index.php/global/article/view/103).

Family knowledge is another resource. Johnson and Johnson describe a four-month case involving two Latin@ ELL students in a Grade 4 classroom in Washington State. After home visits, the students designed and taught language-arts and science lessons based on their interests and home experiences. Natalia developed animal and fossil projects; Carlos developed automobile and volcano activities. The teacher’s role was facilitative: she helped with grouping, timing, materials, classroom management, and editing while the students prepared much of the work themselves. The authors report increased engagement, metacognitive awareness, confidence, and participation, including interest from thirteen additional students who later proposed their own lessons [Johnson and Johnson on home-school connections and funds of knowledge](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1100968.pdf).

This is a powerful case, but it involved only two focal students and required substantial time, including home visits and preparation outside regular lessons. The transferable principle is not that every teacher must reproduce the exact intervention. It is that teachers should look for students’ real competencies and make those competencies visible in the English classroom.

### 3.6 Creativity and multimodal expression

Creativity in elementary English does not require advanced technology or artistic talent. It can mean choosing a different image for a poem, creating an alternative ending, designing a riddle, deciding how to present information, combining words and drawings, or adapting a familiar story.

The Hong Kong guide recommends stories, poems, songs, drama, role play, puppetry, multimodal text creation, and creative writing. It also describes multimodal literacy as the ability to interpret and create meaning through linguistic, visual, audio, gestural, and spatial modes [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

Digital tools can expand options, but they are not synonymous with empowerment. A 2026 Hong Kong implementation used Padlet-based e-portfolios with 158 Grade 4 male Cantonese-speaking students over eight 30-minute lessons. A qualitative evaluation drew on group interviews with a purposive sample of twenty-five students and identified ownership, engagement with multimodal text, and active participation as key themes [Padlet e-portfolio study](https://doi.org/10.1080/17501229.2026.2658189). The study also notes that portfolio work is time-intensive and that learners may need support with self-reflection.

Digital storytelling evidence is mixed. In North Bali, twenty-one students from Grades 4–6 and three English teachers participated in an interpretative phenomenological case study. Students perceived digital storytelling positively and associated it with motivation, participation, vocabulary learning, comprehension, and collaboration. Teachers also reported challenges in content selection, preparation time, learner diversity, technology, and classroom management [Wahyuni, Ratminingsih, and Santosa on digital storytelling](https://e-journal.hamzanwadi.ac.id/index.php/veles/article/view/31917).

A different study in Aseer, Saudi Arabia, used a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design with thirty Grade 4 students, fifteen receiving digital storytelling and fifteen using printed stories. After adjustment for pre-test performance, comprehension means were 11.24 for the digital-storytelling group and 10.09 for the control group, with reported Cohen’s $`d = 0.81`$. Vocabulary means were 9.00 and 7.61, with $`d = 0.39`$, but the vocabulary difference was not statistically significant. The authors caution that the study had a small, single-region sample and no a priori power analysis [Frontiers in Psychology study of digital storytelling](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1825184).

The conclusion is not that digital storytelling works or fails. It is that multimodal tools may support comprehension, ownership, and engagement, while particular language outcomes depend on exposure, task design, vocabulary recycling, sample size, and assessment.

### 3.7 Teacher empowerment and professional judgment

A paradigm that empowers learners but leaves teachers isolated, overloaded, and controlled by unclear requirements is not sustainable.

Teacher empowerment means that teachers have the professional knowledge, time, collaboration, and authority to adapt curriculum responsibly. It does not mean that every teacher works alone according to personal preference. It means that teachers can interpret evidence, understand learners, adjust materials, collect classroom evidence, and explain their decisions.

Aqajani Delavar, Hashemi, and Karimi studied ten English teachers participating in an action-research engagement programme. Interviews and reflective journals indicated changes in teachers’ perceptions of agency and stronger agency in classroom practice [Aqajani Delavar, Hashemi, and Karimi on teacher agency and action research](https://doi.org/10.14221/1835-517x.6608). Dajani’s participatory action-research project involved approximately forty English-language teachers in thirty Palestinian schools and reported effects on classroom practice, professional development, collaboration, and cooperation [Dajani on action research and reflection](https://doi.org/10.14221/1835-517x.6608).

These studies concern teacher development rather than a direct elementary-English empowerment intervention. Their value lies in showing that reflective inquiry can turn teachers from passive implementers into professional investigators.

Classroom management also requires professional judgment. Deaton’s multiple-case study of two experienced science teachers found that they had similar goals but managed classrooms differently, along a continuum from student-centred to teacher-centred practice [Deaton on experienced teachers’ reflective classroom management](https://doi.org/10.1080/14623943.2012.749229). The transferable lesson for English teachers is that there is no single correct amount of teacher control. Management must fit the learners, task, room, time, and purpose.

## 4. Comparing the Paradigm with Actual Alternatives

The comparison below uses ideal types. It does not claim that every conventional lesson or every holistic lesson fits one column.

| Shared axis | Narrow topic-, skill-, or drill-oriented tendency | Holistic empowerment tendency | Resulting judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Learning goal | Remember forms, facts, and correct answers | Use language to understand, communicate, transfer, and act | Explicit form teaching remains necessary but should serve meaningful use |
| Power and participation | Teacher controls topic, turn-taking, response, and evaluation | Teacher structures access while learners exercise bounded choice and responsibility | Agency requires scaffolding rather than absence of direction |
| Language and content | English is practised as an isolated subject | English is integrated with concepts, content, cognition, and culture | Integration is valuable when language support remains visible |
| Student interaction | Recitation, individual completion, or teacher-student exchange | Pair work, group problem solving, peer mediation, and authentic audiences | Collaboration must be explicitly taught and monitored |
| Learner diversity | Same input, process, product, and test for most learners | Differentiated input, multimodal access, flexible output, targeted support | Inclusion fails if assessment remains uniform |
| Assessment | Final product, test score, or error count | Diagnostic, formative, performance, peer, self, conference, and portfolio evidence | Diverse evidence gives a fuller picture but increases planning demands |
| Culture and family | Generic or textbook-only content | Local culture, funds of knowledge, home language, family and community resources | Context increases relevance but requires care, time, and resource development |
| Teacher learning | One-time training or individual adaptation | Mentoring, collaborative inquiry, action research, and PLCs | Sustained support is more plausible than isolated workshops |
| Technology | Digital tool added to an existing worksheet | Technology used selectively for creation, feedback, access, or communication | Low-tech alternatives must remain available |

### 4.1 Teacher control versus learner agency

The false version of empowerment says that the teacher should stop directing learning. That approach can produce noise, unequal participation, and superficial choice. The stronger version retains teacher authority over safety, time, language access, learning goals, and feedback while sharing authority over examples, questions, roles, products, and interpretations.

For example, a teacher may require every child to practise the structure “I recommend ___ because ___.” Children may then choose which food, book, place, or environmental action to recommend. The teacher has not surrendered the language objective; the children have gained meaningful control over the content and audience.

### 4.2 Language-only instruction versus integrated learning

Content integration can make language memorable, but it can also overload learners. A Grade 4 child may have enough English to describe a familiar food but not enough to understand an abstract nutrition article without visuals, a word bank, sentence frames, and oral rehearsal.

The practical comparison is therefore not “language or content.” It is “content with language support or content without support.” The Taiwanese concept-based study and the CLIL 4Cs model show why conceptual richness must be matched by scaffolding.

### 4.3 Individual work versus collaborative learning

Group work is not automatically empowering. One confident child may speak while others decorate. A group may divide tasks without discussing ideas. Collaboration becomes educational when students have interdependent roles, shared criteria, language for negotiation, and individual evidence of contribution.

The Grade 6 teacher in Sleman described projects as requiring students to discuss ideas, negotiate roles, solve problems together, and repeat oral communication. The same teacher also reported low initial engagement, declining writing skills, extended time requirements, and the need for a strict timeline and active teacher feedback [Rukadah and Raihana on project-based English teaching](https://ejournal.uin-suska.ac.id/index.php/IJIELT/article/download/36606/13484).

The judgment is therefore conditional: collaboration can increase communication, but only if the teacher designs participation rather than merely placing children into groups.

### 4.4 Standardized assessment versus process-sensitive assessment

Standardized tests can provide useful information about certain language outcomes. They are efficient for comparing performance on defined skills. They are less suitable for assessing confidence, collaboration, creativity, identity, strategy use, or progress made through revision.

The Hong Kong guide recommends extending assessment for learning to assessment as learning, involving students in goal-setting, reflection, peer feedback, portfolios, conferences, and project assessment. It also provides templates for intervention programmes, project learning, peer assessment, self-assessment, portfolios, oral presentations, group discussion, and collaborative work [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, assessment appendices](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

The challenge is not to eliminate tests but to prevent them from becoming the only legitimate evidence.

## 5. Frontline Classroom Practices and Documented Teaching Scenarios

The following section distinguishes documented cases from illustrative adaptations. The documented cases are attributed to their sources. The proposed lesson routines and adaptations are professional syntheses for novice teachers, not claims about an unreported personal classroom or experimentally validated intervention.

### 5.1 Documented case: the English Menu Design project

Guo and Wang describe a Grade 4 project based on PEP Primary English Grade 4, Unit 7, “My Food.” Students worked on an “English Menu Design for Campus Food Festival” project. They collected information about food, practised vocabulary such as hamburger, salad, and juice, used the structure “I like…,” considered nutrition and popularity, created bilingual posters, and presented healthy recommendations [Guo and Wang on project-based primary English education](https://www.francis-press.com/uploads/papers/CiPf4dcz8Khxl25VQ0ouHNYWOwvsSGjUC4galvDK.pdf).

The activity demonstrates several empowerment mechanisms:

- Vocabulary has a communicative purpose.
- Students use language to make a recommendation rather than merely identify a picture.
- Nutrition creates a reason to compare and evaluate.
- Group work creates a need for negotiation.
- The bilingual poster connects English with a real school audience.
- Presentation makes language, reasoning, and design visible.

A novice teacher could simplify the project by using three foods, one sentence frame, and a single poster section per group. The aim is not to reproduce the whole project but to preserve the mechanism: language is needed to make and communicate a decision.

### 5.2 Documented case: descriptive-text projects and presentation

Astuti and colleagues report a qualitative case in an Indonesian elementary EFL setting where a teacher implemented project-based learning through descriptive-text projects, visual-aid creation, and public presentations involving teachers, classmates, and parents. The teacher perceived that students organized information, expressed ideas, communicated authentically, developed confidence, and became more motivated and participatory. The same teacher identified varying proficiency levels, limited time, and presentation anxiety as practical challenges [Astuti and colleagues on project-based elementary EFL learning](https://pub.siradjournal.com/index.php/react/article/view/159).

The case is valuable because it places benefits and constraints together. A project can offer authentic communication while also increasing anxiety. The teacher’s role is therefore not to require immediate public performance from every child. A sensible progression might be:

1. individual planning with pictures and word banks;
2. oral rehearsal with a partner;
3. small-group presentation;
4. optional recorded presentation or poster explanation;
5. whole-class presentation for students who are ready.

The language objective remains common, but the route to public performance is differentiated.

### 5.3 Documented case: the Grade 6 project-based learning account

Rukadah and Raihana studied a Grade 6 class taught by an English teacher with twenty years of experience in a private elementary school in Sleman. The qualitative case used a semi-structured interview and daily reflection journals. The teacher associated project work with engagement, group responsibility, teamwork, negotiation of roles, problem solving, repeated speaking, and growing confidence among initially hesitant students [Rukadah and Raihana](https://ejournal.uin-suska.ac.id/index.php/IJIELT/article/download/36606/13484).

The teacher also reported difficulties: low initial engagement, weakening writing skills, extended time, the need for a consistent timeline, and the need for active monitoring and feedback. This is precisely the kind of frontline evidence novice teachers need. A method can be educationally worthwhile and still fail if its time demands, writing support, and progress checks are neglected.

### 5.4 Documented case: digital multimodal composing

A 2026 study involved twenty-five Grade 5 students in a four-week interdisciplinary Social Studies and English project on children’s human rights. The project used Problem-Based Learning as its theme, integrated Task-Based Language Teaching, included five instructional stages, and used a three-stage writing process of planning, drafting, and revising. Task repetition was used to separate multimodal complexity from linguistic difficulty [Digital Multimodal Composing study](https://doi.org/10.25231/pee.2026.32.1.103).

The analysis reported that interaction developed from tool-mediated activity toward critical dialogue and language-related episodes involving collaborative vocabulary refinement and translanguaging. Gallery walks with rotating roles created opportunities for linguistic, visual, and multimodal peer feedback and supported metacognitive reflection.

This case illustrates a sophisticated principle: technology should not replace language interaction. It should create new reasons to interact. The device becomes educationally useful when children must decide what to say, how to represent it, how to revise it, and how to respond to an audience.

The study reports positive learner perceptions of digital-literacy development, critical thinking, and authentic language use, but no numerical survey results or controlled learning estimate. It is therefore evidence of process and perception, not a definitive achievement claim.

### 5.5 Documented case: storytelling, role play, games, and multimedia

Ratnadimarta reports a six-week practice-based initiative using storytelling, role play, interactive games, and multimedia tools in elementary English learning. Classroom observations, student feedback, reflective journals, and teacher-student interactions were used. The report describes increased engagement, motivation, meaningful real-life use of English, participation, confidence, self-expression, and student agency [Ratnadimarta on creative methods in elementary English learning](https://doi.org/10.61105/jise.v3i1.180).

The source does not state a sample size or comparison condition. Its value is practitioner evidence showing how creative routines may alter participation and classroom relationships. The proper conclusion is not that the methods “significantly” improve all outcomes, but that they offer adaptable routes into meaningful language use that merit careful classroom observation.

### 5.6 Documented case: poetry, portfolios, and conferences

Holy Family Canossian School in Hong Kong conducted a collaborative P6 research-and-development project with planning, implementation, and evaluation stages. It combined writing portfolios, self-directed learning, writing conferences, and parent feedback. In a poem task, students selected images such as a rainbow, cake, candle, or flower to describe a friend, wrote with similes or metaphors, rehearsed one stanza in pairs, completed the rest independently, and self-evaluated [Holy Family Canossian School school-based writing and assessment project](https://cd1.edb.hkedcity.net/cd/languagesupport/sbcp/attachments/1618_en_case05.pdf).

A pre-test/post-test comparison reported that more than 70% of students achieved three or four marks out of five for content, while the proportion receiving one or two marks fell from 42% to 27%. The report interprets this as improvement in content and elaboration of ideas. The evidence comes from one school project, so it cannot establish that the portfolio system alone caused the change. It does show how personal expression, rehearsal, independent writing, self-evaluation, and conferencing can be combined in a manageable writing sequence.

### 5.7 A practical elementary task: “My Favourite Toy”

The Hong Kong guide provides a lower-primary task in which each child brings or chooses a toy, participates in a guessing game, uses picture dictionaries or word books, writes a description, rehearses in a group, and takes part in show-and-tell. The language includes names and parts of toys, size words, “It has…,” “This is…,” and “I like…” [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, Sample Tasks](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

The task is empowering because the object is personal, the vocabulary is functional, and the presentation can occur first in a small group. It is also inclusive: a child may draw the toy, point to a labelled picture, read a sentence frame, or produce several original sentences depending on readiness.

A novice teacher should not interpret the task as “let children speak freely.” The teacher needs to model description, provide a word bank, rehearse pronunciation, teach how to ask and answer questions, manage turn-taking, and decide how to respond to errors without interrupting every sentence.

### 5.8 Management during collaborative tasks

Holistic tasks often fail through preventable management problems rather than weak educational intentions. The teacher should plan:

- how groups will form;
- where materials will be collected;
- which student will distribute and return resources;
- how long each phase will last;
- what voice level is appropriate;
- what students do when they finish;
- how a student requests help;
- how the teacher checks individual participation;
- what happens when a group cannot agree.

The Hong Kong guide’s classroom-interaction resources provide language for group work, including “Do you agree?”, “Any suggestions?”, “It’s my turn,” “Your turn, please,” “Can you help me?”, and “How do you say that in English?” [English for Classroom Interaction, Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

Group roles should be taught rather than assumed. A simple group of four might include a discussion leader, materials manager, language helper, and reporter. Roles should rotate, and the teacher should collect individual evidence through observation, short reflection, or a brief individual performance.

## 6. Practical Implementation Guidance for Novice Teachers

The following progression is an evidence-informed synthesis, not a directly evaluated novice-teacher intervention. It is designed to be manageable under ordinary conditions.

### 6.1 Begin with a minimum viable holistic lesson

A novice teacher does not need to redesign the whole curriculum immediately. Begin with four commitments:

1. one clear language objective;
2. one structured opportunity for student choice;
3. one meaningful interaction;
4. one short reflection or feedback moment.

For example, the language objective may be “Students can use ‘I recommend… because…’ to express a preference.” The empowerment dimension may be agency. Students choose one school snack, rehearse with a partner, recommend it to a small group, and complete the sentence “I chose ___ because ___.”

This lesson is small enough to manage and rich enough to reveal how children respond to choice, rehearsal, interaction, and reflection.

### 6.2 A seven-stage progression

#### Stage 1: Establish safety and diagnose needs

Begin with predictable greetings, seating, signals, classroom English, partner routines, and a short diagnostic activity. Observe not only written knowledge but also listening, speaking, confidence, attention, interaction, and response to instructions.

The Hong Kong guide’s intervention template recommends collecting evidence from listening and speaking as well as written work and considering motivation, confidence, learning style, and understanding of instructions [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, intervention programme template](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

A useful diagnostic is not a long test. It may be a picture description, a short partner exchange, a listening-and-do task, or a shared reading observation.

#### Stage 2: Choose one language objective and one empowerment dimension

Do not attempt to assess every dimension in every lesson. Select one primary language objective and one additional focus.

Examples:

- speaking plus confidence;
- reading plus strategy use;
- writing plus revision;
- vocabulary plus collaboration;
- listening plus empathy;
- grammar plus purposeful communication.

This prevents “holistic” from becoming so broad that no one knows what is being taught.

#### Stage 3: Provide comprehensible input and visible scaffolds

Before asking children to perform, provide the language they need. Use pictures, real objects, gestures, short model texts, sentence frames, word banks, bilingual resources where appropriate, and teacher think-aloud.

Scaffolding should be temporary and adjustable. A beginner may receive a complete sentence frame; a more advanced learner may receive only key vocabulary. The goal is not to make every child produce identical language, but to enable every child to work toward the same meaningful purpose.

#### Stage 4: Rehearse privately before public performance

Pair rehearsal is one of the most efficient ways to reduce anxiety. Children can practise with a partner, then in a group of four, before presenting to the whole class. A child who is not yet ready for live presentation may submit an audio recording, point to a poster while a partner speaks, or present to the teacher.

This is not lowering expectations. It is sequencing risk.

#### Stage 5: Create an authentic response

The response may be a short oral recommendation, a labelled drawing, a riddle, a role play, a class survey, a poster, a poem, a set of instructions, a recorded message, or a mini-exhibition.

The task should give children a reason to use English. “Write five sentences” is a language exercise. “Write a message inviting a friend to the school festival” creates an audience and purpose.

#### Stage 6: Collect formative evidence

While children work, observe:

- who understands the task;
- who uses the target language;
- who needs vocabulary;
- who dominates;
- who withdraws;
- which group roles function;
- which misconception is emerging;
- which support makes participation possible.

Do not try to mark everything. Record one or two useful observations per group and use them to plan the next lesson.

#### Stage 7: Reflect before expanding

Ask children a small number of questions:

- What did you learn to say or write?
- What choice did you make?
- Who helped you?
- What was difficult?
- What will you try next time?

When the routine is stable, extend it into a short project with a beginning, middle, product, and reflection.

### 6.3 A 40-minute sample lesson routine

The following is an illustrative routine for a mixed-ability Grade 4 class working on food recommendations.

| Time | Teacher and student activity | Empowerment purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 0–3 minutes | Greeting, visual agenda, emotional or readiness check | Predictability and belonging |
| 3–10 minutes | Teacher models a short dialogue about two foods using pictures | Comprehensible input |
| 10–15 minutes | Students notice vocabulary and the frame “I prefer ___ because ___” | Language awareness |
| 15–23 minutes | Pair rehearsal with word cards and sentence frames | Low-risk participation |
| 23–33 minutes | Groups choose one food and create a recommendation card | Bounded choice and collaboration |
| 33–38 minutes | Groups share with another group or present briefly | Authentic communication |
| 38–40 minutes | Exit reflection: “I said…,” “I helped…,” “Next time…” | Assessment as learning |

This routine is not presented as a validated intervention. It is a manageable way to combine explicit teaching, interaction, choice, product, and reflection.

### 6.4 A planning template

Before teaching, a novice teacher can complete the following template.

| Planning question | Example |
|---|---|
| What must students learn in English? | Use “I recommend… because…” |
| What will make the language necessary? | Recommend one food for a school event |
| What will I model? | A two-line dialogue and one completed card |
| What choices can students make? | Food, reason, drawing, partner role |
| What support will some learners need? | Pictures, bilingual word bank, sentence frames |
| How will every student participate? | Pair rehearsal, rotating roles, individual exit response |
| What evidence will I collect? | Oral observation, card, self-reflection |
| What will I change next lesson? | Add vocabulary or shorten the task |

### 6.5 Adapting to common constraints

| Constraint | Practical adaptation | Trade-off to monitor |
|---|---|---|
| Limited English proficiency | Use visuals, gestures, repeated story language, sentence frames, and home-language resources | Support should gradually reduce rather than become permanent dependence |
| Large class | Use fixed groups, rotating roles, peer rehearsal, visible timers, and group reporting | Group work can hide individual learning |
| Limited technology | Replace digital stories with paper storyboards, printed photos, puppets, or teacher-recorded audio | Preserve multimodal meaning without requiring devices |
| Mixed proficiency | Vary input, support, expected output, and extension while retaining a shared purpose | Differentiation should not become low expectations for some learners |
| Presentation anxiety | Rehearse privately, use small audiences, allow recording or paired presentation | Avoid forcing public performance as the only proof of learning |
| Special educational needs | Offer multiple ways to receive instructions and respond; coordinate targeted support | Consult relevant specialists and avoid assuming one strategy suits all |
| Limited time | Use a one-lesson task or a two-lesson mini-project with a fixed product | Large projects may crowd out foundational language teaching |
| Heavy marking load | Use one or two criteria per task, peer feedback, oral conferences, and sample-based marking | Feedback must remain specific and actionable |

### 6.6 Inclusion through MTSS

A practical elementary English version of MTSS may look like this:

- Tier 1: all students receive clear modelling, visuals, predictable routines, partner talk, accessible texts, and formative checks.
- Tier 2: selected students receive short additional practice in pronunciation, spelling, vocabulary, reading, confidence, or task interpretation.
- Tier 3: individual students receive intensive, coordinated support based on specific learning needs and specialist advice.

The Hong Kong guide similarly recommends short, focused intervention with additional time, additional opportunities, and focused learning. It advises teachers to diagnose problems through multiple sources of evidence and to avoid overwhelming learners with repeated mechanical drilling [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, Appendix 12](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

### 6.7 Classroom management as empowerment

Empowerment is impossible without order, but order should be taught as a condition for participation rather than imposed only as obedience.

A novice teacher can establish:

- a visual sequence for each lesson;
- a consistent attention signal;
- a limited number of voice-level expectations;
- a materials routine;
- group roles;
- a help signal;
- a method for changing partners;
- a time warning;
- a short reflection on how well the group worked.

When a group becomes noisy, the teacher should diagnose the cause. Is the task unclear? Are materials inaccessible? Is there no role for one child? Is the language demand too high? Is the group too large? Discipline may be necessary, but instructional redesign is often part of the solution.

### 6.8 From first lesson to sustained practice

A realistic progression for a novice teacher is:

- Weeks 1–2: routines, diagnostic observation, partner rehearsal, short oral responses.
- Weeks 3–4: one choice-based task per week, with a simple reflection.
- Weeks 5–6: process writing, peer feedback, or a small presentation.
- Weeks 7–8: a two- or three-lesson mini-project with group roles.
- Later: portfolio development, cross-curricular tasks, community or family connections, and teacher inquiry.

This sequence is proposed because novice teachers commonly need to learn classroom management, curriculum interpretation, parent communication, reporting, school culture, and instructional planning simultaneously. A case study of elementary-school mentoring found that novices relied on mentors for parent conferences, classroom management, curriculum content, progress reports, staff relationships, and school culture [Supporting Novice Teachers Through Mentoring and Induction in Elementary Schools](http://hdl.handle.net/10919/111209).

### 6.9 Mentoring and collaborative teacher learning

Mentoring should not be limited to occasional advice after a problem occurs. It should include regularly scheduled meetings, co-planning, observation, evidence review, and reflective conversation. The mentoring case study identified support, accessibility, and collaboration as factors affecting mentoring programmes and reported that scheduled meetings and check-ins gave mentors and novices time to work through practical issues.

Ardila and Nisa’s narrative inquiry into one novice English teacher’s first year in a public elementary school identified classroom and emotional-management difficulties alongside professional growth. The authors recommend emotional preparation, reflective practice, institutional mentoring, and ongoing professional development [Ardila and Nisa on novice elementary English teachers](https://doi.org/10.30762/sittah.v6i2.6816).

Evidence about mentoring should still be interpreted carefully. Whalen, Majocha, and Van Nuland studied six novice teachers during their first three years in Canada and found a gap between the theoretical expectation that mentoring improves retention and the evidence collected in their study [Whalen, Majocha, and Van Nuland on novice teacher mentorship](https://doi.org/10.1080/02619768.2019.1652906). Mentoring availability alone is not proof of effectiveness; its quality, accessibility, trust, and relevance matter.

A networked professional learning community offers one promising structure. He, Kroiss, and Bernal De La Ossa describe a year-long project involving twenty-six educators across eleven districts, organized into five virtual PLCs. Participants engaged in monthly ninety-minute meetings for eight months, used a cycle of reviewing practice, defining goals, comparing alternatives, experimenting, and reflecting, and worked on multilingual family engagement [Networked professional learning communities for multilingual family engagement](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10833-025-09530-7).

The study reported that educators challenged one-way communication with families and explored reciprocal, asset-based engagement. It involved one U.S. state and only eight elementary educators, so it is not a direct test of novice elementary English development. It does, however, support the practical value of sustained professional dialogue across roles and schools.

## 7. Assessment, Evidence, Challenges, and Reflective Improvement

### 7.1 Assessment must follow the learning purpose

If holistic empowerment includes language, agency, collaboration, creativity, inclusion, and reflection, one short written test cannot represent the entire learning process. Nor should teachers create an enormous assessment system that becomes impossible to manage.

The solution is alignment. Each lesson or project should identify:

- what students are learning;
- what evidence would show that learning;
- who will collect the evidence;
- how the evidence will inform the next step.

The Hong Kong guide describes assessment as part of the learning-teaching-assessment cycle. It distinguishes:

- assessment of learning, which summarizes attainment;
- assessment for learning, which gives teachers and students information for improvement; and
- assessment as learning, which involves students in monitoring, evaluating, and planning their own learning [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, Chapter 5](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

### 7.2 A balanced evidence system

| Evidence source | What it can show | What it cannot establish by itself |
|---|---|---|
| Language task or test | Performance in listening, speaking, reading, writing, vocabulary, or grammar | Confidence, belonging, or long-term transfer |
| Teacher observation | Participation, strategy use, interaction, persistence, and support needs | A fully objective measure without clear criteria |
| Student artifact | Language use, ideas, organization, revision, creativity, and content understanding | Whether the child completed all work independently |
| Portfolio | Progress across drafts, modes, and time; reflection and ownership | A standardized comparison unless criteria are carefully defined |
| Peer assessment | Understanding of criteria, listening, feedback, and collaboration | Reliable judgment without modelling and practice |
| Self-assessment | Perceived confidence, strategy use, goals, and reflection | Actual proficiency without performance evidence |
| Conference | Reasoning, misconceptions, goals, and next steps | A scalable measure for every child in every lesson |
| Family or community feedback | Authenticity, relevance, and connection beyond school | Direct attribution of academic improvement |

### 7.3 Assessing language and empowerment together

A project rubric can use four dimensions:

1. language: vocabulary, comprehensibility, sentence control, fluency, or text organization;
2. meaning: relevance, clarity, content understanding, or reasoning;
3. process: planning, revision, strategy use, and response to feedback;
4. participation: collaboration, listening, responsibility, respect, and confidence.

The teacher does not need to give equal weight to all four dimensions. The rubric should reflect the stated learning purpose. A speaking task may prioritize meaning and fluency over grammatical accuracy. A final edited report may place more emphasis on organization and language control.

The Hong Kong guide provides generic feedback sheets for oral presentation, group discussion, writing, group projects, and collaborative work. Its project guidance explicitly recommends assessing both process and product, including content, organization, language, generic skills, and attitudes [Hong Kong English Language Curriculum Guide, project and assessment appendices](https://www.edb.gov.hk/attachment/en/curriculum-development/kla/eng-edu/Curriculum%20Document/Pri_ELCG_Primary_1-6_2025.pdf).

### 7.4 Portfolio assessment

A portfolio should not be a collection of everything a child has done. It is a purposeful selection showing development.

A manageable elementary English portfolio might contain:

- one early writing sample;
- one revised writing sample;
- one oral recording or teacher observation;
- one reading response;
- one project artifact;
- one peer-feedback sheet;
- one student reflection;
- one short goal for the next cycle.

Students can explain why they selected an item, what changed, and what they still want to improve. This gives agency a visible form without turning the concept into a vague personality score.

### 7.5 What the evidence actually shows

The evidence base contains several different kinds of claims and should not treat them as equivalent.

| Evidence level | Examples | Strongest justified conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Official curriculum or policy | Hong Kong guide, whole-child frameworks, district assessment guidance | Establishes aims, recommended practices, and system expectations |
| Conceptual framework | Tsai’s four-part framework; agency and multiliteracies models | Clarifies constructs and suggests design principles |
| Qualitative case study | Indonesian PBL cases, North Bali digital storytelling, P6 portfolio work | Shows how practices are experienced and implemented in context |
| Practice-based action report | Ratnadimarta’s six-week creative methods | Documents practitioner observations and adaptations |
| Quasi-experimental study | ABL with fifty students; Saudi digital storytelling with thirty students; Vietnam SEL-English study | Provides bounded comparisons or pre/post evidence, with design limitations |
| Systematic or umbrella review | Storytelling review of seventy-five articles; differentiated-instruction review; science SEL review | Identifies trends across studies, but may combine different populations and methods |
| Teacher-development study | AREP, Dajani, PLCs, mentoring studies | Shows how professional learning and agency may develop, not necessarily student achievement |

The distinction matters. A conceptual framework may be useful without being validated. A qualitative study may reveal a mechanism without estimating its size. A quasi-experiment may show a difference without establishing long-term transfer. An official guide may recommend a practice without proving its effectiveness.

### 7.6 Evidence conflicts and what they mean

#### Digital storytelling

North Bali students reported positive perceptions of digital storytelling, while the Saudi quasi-experiment found a large comprehension effect but no statistically significant vocabulary difference. The apparent conflict disappears when the outcomes are separated. Digital storytelling may support comprehension, engagement, multimodal meaning-making, and confidence, while vocabulary growth may require repeated, deliberate recycling over a longer period.

#### Project-based learning

The Indonesian cases describe motivation, participation, confidence, authentic communication, and collaboration. They also report time pressure, proficiency differences, presentation anxiety, unclear guidance, workload, and product-focused assessment. The judgment is not that PBL is inherently effective or ineffective. Its success depends on scope, staging, language support, role design, monitoring, and assessment.

#### Differentiation and UDL

The West Lombok study reports higher engagement, self-esteem, participation, literacy, and positive character qualities after differentiated instruction, while also reporting insufficient training, resources, time, manageable class size, and organizational support. The Yogyakarta UDL case shows that teachers may use multiple means of engagement and representation while retaining standardized written tests. Inclusion requires alignment across teaching and assessment.

#### Mentoring

Policy and theory often recommend mentoring, but the six-participant Canadian study found a gap between expected retention benefits and observed practice. Mentoring is therefore a condition that must be designed and supported, not a guaranteed solution.

### 7.7 Reflective improvement through action research

A novice teacher can use a modest action-research cycle without turning the classroom into a formal experiment.
